summary: Extends the IPsec Domain of Interpretation for ISAKMP so that two ends can negotiate whether to use traditional 32-bit sequence numbers or extended 64-bit sequence numbers to detect replays in AH or ESP. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4304 defines an ISAKMP attribute that lets IPsec peers negotiate 64-bit extended sequence numbers for AH or ESP. The larger sequence space supports more packets on a security association before sequence-number exhaustion.

questions: what is ipsec extended sequence number
how do ipsec peers negotiate 64-bit sequence numbers
what are ipsec extended sequence numbers
subtitle: How IPsec peers negotiate whether to use 64-bit extended sequence numbers.

tldr.problem: IPsec's traditional 32-bit sequence numbers can be exhausted when a security association carries very large amounts of data at high speed.
tldr.mechanism: The IPsec DOI adds a Phase II security-association attribute that indicates use of 64-bit extended sequence numbers during IKE negotiation.
tldr.outcome: The extension allows peers to negotiate extended numbering for AH or ESP, while requiring the association setup to stop if unsupported attribute values are received.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 4304's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC defines a negotiation attribute for extended sequence numbers in IPsec security associations.

sections.title: Why Use Extended Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
IPsec Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload use sequence numbers to detect replayed packets. Their extended sequence number option allows very large volumes of data to pass over one security association without rekeying just to avoid sequence-number exhaustion.

This RFC describes the additions to the IPsec Domain of Interpretation for ISAKMP needed to negotiate the option during IKE.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec uses sequence numbers to recognize replayed packets. Extended sequence numbers let a connection count farther before it runs out of numbers.

sections.title: Negotiating the Sequence Number Size
sections.content:
The RFC defines a basic security-association attribute with type value 11. Its class value 1 means the association uses 64-bit sequence numbers; value 0 is reserved.

If an implementation receives a defined attribute or value it does not support, it should send an ATTRIBUTES-NOT-SUPPORT response and must abort security-association setup. Any value other than the defined 64-bit choice also requires the setup to be aborted.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers use an attribute to agree on the extended sequence-number option. If a peer does not understand the requested value, the security association must not be set up.

sections.title: Other Cryptographic Limits Still Apply
sections.content:
The RFC says the attribute does not change IKE's underlying security characteristics. However, algorithms used with an extended sequence number must remain secure for the amount of data protected under one key.

For example, the memo says DES in CBC mode is unsuitable for more than 2^32 blocks under one key. A security-association lifetime can limit protected traffic before reaching the extended sequence-number limit.
sections.plainLanguage: A larger sequence number does not make every encryption choice safe for unlimited data. The amount protected by a key still needs to stay within the algorithm's limits.
